title: Unit of Work Pattern
oneLiner: Tracks every change made during a business operation and commits them all together, as one atomic transaction — or none at all.

hero.name: The Ledger
hero.catchphrase: Every change gets tracked. Nothing commits until it ALL commits together.
hero.power: Tracks every change made across multiple objects during a business operation, committing them as a single atomic transaction, or rolling all of them back.
hero.weakness: Real bookkeeping overhead, and easy to misuse if some changes bypass the tracked unit of work entirely — a stray direct save() silently breaks the all-or-nothing guarantee.
hero.origin: The Ledger appeared after a 'transfer funds' operation debited one account, then crashed before crediting the other — leaving the money simply gone, with two separate untracked save() calls, neither aware of the other's fate.

story.problem: `transferFunds()` saves the debit to Account A, then crashes before saving the credit to Account B. The two `save()` calls are entirely independent — nothing ties them together, so the money is simply gone.
story.solution: The Ledger introduces a `UnitOfWork` that registers both changes, then commits them together in a single transaction. If anything fails before commit, nothing is saved at all — not the debit, not the credit.
story.result: A crash mid-transfer now leaves the database exactly as it was before the operation started. Either both changes land, or neither does — money is never silently lost.

before: Each change is saved independently, as it happens
A crash mid-operation can leave data partially updated
No single point tracks everything that changed together
after: All changes are registered, then committed together as one unit
A crash before commit leaves the database completely unchanged
One clear point tracks and commits every related change

panels.label: The Problem
panels.caption: A production incident report shows $500 debited from one account, with no matching credit anywhere — the transfer crashed halfway.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: The debit saved, then the app crashed before the credit saved. Five hundred dollars just... vanished from the system.

panels.label: The Hero Arrives
panels.caption: The Ledger appears holding a single open book, tracking every pending change before a single one is finalized.
panels.speaker: The Ledger
panels.dialogue: Stop saving changes one at a time. Register them all with me first — I'll commit them together, or not at all.

panels.label: Pattern Power
panels.caption: unitOfWork.registerDirty(accountA); unitOfWork.registerDirty(accountB); unitOfWork.commit() saves both in one transaction.
panels.speaker: The Ledger
panels.dialogue: Both changes commit together, in one transaction. If anything fails before commit(), neither change is saved — not one, not the other.

panels.label: The Result
panels.caption: The same crash scenario now leaves both accounts exactly as they were before the transfer started.
panels.speaker: Developer
panels.dialogue: Same crash, but now neither account changed at all. The money never left in the first place — no partial state, ever.

useWhen: A single business operation touches multiple objects that must be saved together, atomically, or not at all.
You need to guarantee data consistency even if the operation fails partway through.
You want to batch several changes into one database round-trip instead of many separate saves.
avoidWhen: Operations only ever touch a single object — a simple save() with no coordination is enough.
The underlying data store doesn't support real transactions, making the 'all or nothing' guarantee hard to actually deliver.
The added bookkeeping (tracking dirty entities, coordinating commit) isn't worth it for genuinely simple, low-risk operations.
commonMistakes: Letting some code call save() directly, bypassing the Unit of Work entirely and silently breaking the all-or-nothing guarantee.
Forgetting to roll back cleanly on failure, leaving the tracked entities in an inconsistent in-memory state even if the database itself rolled back correctly.
Keeping a Unit of Work alive across too large or too long an operation, risking long-held locks or stale tracked state.
Confusing Unit of Work with a database transaction itself — Unit of Work is the application-level tracking and coordination; the transaction is the underlying mechanism it relies on.
explanation.realWorldExample: ORM 'session' or 'change tracking' objects (like Entity Framework's DbContext or Hibernate's Session) that batch and commit changes together are real-world Unit of Work implementations — most modern ORMs implement this pattern under the hood.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: Isn't this just... a database transaction?

conversation.speaker: The Ledger
conversation.message: The database transaction is the underlying mechanism, yes. I'm the APPLICATION-LEVEL bookkeeping on top of it — tracking which objects changed across a whole business operation, so they all get wrapped in that transaction together.

conversation.speaker: Mentor
conversation.message: What's the easiest way to break your guarantee?

conversation.speaker: The Ledger
conversation.message: One stray direct save() call that bypasses me entirely. The moment any change happens outside my tracking, the all-or-nothing promise is broken — even if everything else does it correctly.

codeBattle.scenario: Your order-processing system needs to deduct inventory, charge the customer, and create a shipment record — and a recent outage during step two left inventory deducted with no charge and no shipment, corrupting the data.
codeBattle.question: Which hero should you call?
codeBattle.explanation: The Ledger tracks the inventory deduction, charge, and shipment creation together, committing all three atomically — a crash mid-operation leaves none of them applied.

quiz.question: What guarantee does Unit of Work provide?
options: All tracked changes commit together as one atomic operation, or none of them do
Each change is saved immediately as it happens
Only the first tracked change is ever saved
Changes are saved in a random order
quiz.answer: All tracked changes commit together as one atomic operation, or none of them do
quiz.explanation: This all-or-nothing guarantee is exactly what prevents partial, corrupted writes.

quiz.question: What's the easiest way to accidentally break Unit of Work's guarantee?
options: Letting some code save an entity directly, bypassing the tracked unit of work entirely
Registering too many entities as dirty
Using it with a database that supports transactions
quiz.answer: Letting some code save an entity directly, bypassing the tracked unit of work entirely
quiz.explanation: Any change made outside the Unit of Work's tracking isn't included in the atomic commit, silently breaking the guarantee.

quiz.question: How does Unit of Work relate to a database transaction?
options: Unit of Work is application-level tracking and coordination built on top of an underlying database transaction
A database transaction requires Unit of Work to exist
Unit of Work replaces the need for any database transaction
quiz.answer: Unit of Work is application-level tracking and coordination built on top of an underlying database transaction
quiz.explanation: The transaction provides the atomicity mechanism; Unit of Work tracks which changes should be included in it.

quiz.question: What's a real-world implementation of Unit of Work?
options: An ORM's 'session' or change-tracking object, like Entity Framework's DbContext
A single raw SQL INSERT statement
quiz.answer: An ORM's 'session' or change-tracking object, like Entity Framework's DbContext
quiz.explanation: Most modern ORMs implement Unit of Work under the hood to batch and commit tracked changes together.
